profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for an internal proposal to create a department-wide 'ML-in-SE Research Quality Kit' based on findings from a recent qualitative study of software engineering researchers' ML practices. The kit is intended to support three use cases: a reviewer checklist for paper submissions, a lightweight teaching module for graduate seminars, and a template for research groups documenting ML methodology in SE studies. The proposal already includes a draft architecture with a web-based checklist builder, example case studies, and a small metadata schema for capturing practices like data handling, tuning, and evaluation. The meeting context is that the team must decide whether the proposal is ready to move from concept review into a 6-week implementation sprint before the next methods workshop. The agenda is to review the proposed scope, assess what 'ready for pilot' means, confirm what evidence from the study must be encoded in the first version, and identify any design changes before approval. The expected outcome is a conditional approval of the design with a shared understanding of what the pilot will include and what artifacts must be produced.

members.name: Dr. Lina Morales
members.expertise: ML tooling for empirical software engineering, research infrastructure, prototype-to-pilot transitions
members.background: Lina leads a small research engineering group in a software engineering lab and has previously built internal platforms that turn methodological guidance into usable tools for researchers and reviewers.
members.private_state: She wants approval today so implementation can start immediately, and she is trying to keep the first version narrow enough that her team can deliver it with existing staff while still sounding broadly useful to researchers, reviewers, and instructors.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' means an internal lab deployment with one or two friendly research groups and does not require external-facing polish or broad curricular packaging.
The 'reviewer checklist' is primarily for assessing ML methodology in submitted SE papers, while educational reuse can be handled later through examples rather than standalone teaching assets.

When the proposal says it will 'cover the study findings,' that means representing the main grounded-theory categories and a few illustrative examples, not exhaustively encoding all challenge variants and edge cases.
A 'usable artifact' for the workshop is a functioning prototype with seeded content and manual curation, even if some recommendation logic is still static rather than fully configurable.

members.name: Prof. Ethan Park
members.role: Graduate Program Director and Senior SE Researcher
members.expertise: software engineering methodology, peer review standards, graduate curriculum design
members.background: Ethan oversees the department's methods sequence, regularly reviews ML-for-SE papers for top venues, and often turns research outputs into reusable teaching material for doctoral seminars.
members.private_state: He wants the design to be credible as a community-facing resource that can be shown in the workshop and quickly adopted in courses, but he does not want to sound like he is expanding scope beyond what the team can manage.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' means something polished enough to be shown to external workshop attendees and used by instructors without hand-holding, even if only in a limited setting.
The 'reviewer checklist' naturally includes parallel teaching-facing materials, because review guidance and research-method education are two sides of the same quality problem.

If the proposal claims to be grounded in the study, then the first version should preserve most of the nuance around underused practices, reviewer concerns, and human-in-the-loop evaluation challenges rather than collapsing them into broad buckets.
A design is 'ready' only if the handoff artifacts include concrete usage guidance, sample walkthroughs, and clear interpretation notes so others can apply it consistently.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss getting the design 'ready for pilot' before the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'pilot' means an internal, lightly supported deployment with selected lab users, sufficient to validate the workflow and content structure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'pilot' means a workshop-ready, externally presentable package that can be used by others with minimal guidance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research tooling contexts, 'pilot' often informally refers to an early rollout, so both speakers hear a familiar term and assume the other shares their notion of readiness without needing to unpack audience, polish level, or support expectations.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the reviewer checklist
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the 'reviewer checklist' as a core deliverable.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the checklist covers only peer-review assessment prompts for ML methodology in SE papers, with educational use handled indirectly through examples.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the checklist deliverable also includes instructor-facing framing, discussion prompts, and adaptation for seminar use because the proposal targets review and education together.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A checklist sounds like a single obvious artifact, and in academic settings review and teaching materials are often informally repurposed, so the boundary between the core checklist and companion teaching assets is left unstated.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to cover the findings
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the first version should 'cover the findings from the study.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes coverage is achieved if the tool captures the major categories from the qualitative analysis—such as data handling, tuning, evaluation, and human expertise—with a manageable set of representative prompts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes coverage requires retaining enough granularity to distinguish specific issues like non-functional evaluation, sparse hyperparameter tuning, and reviewer-versus-educator concerns as separate actionable items.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely endorsing fidelity to the same study, and 'cover the findings' sounds naturally sufficient in a design review; the disagreement lies in threshold and granularity, which feels too second-order to restate.

misalignment_points.topic: How the examples will be prepared
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to include 'two worked examples' in the first version.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the examples will be manually authored walkthroughs based on two existing internal papers, embedded as fixed demos in the web tool.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the examples will be reusable teaching packets with discussion notes and interpretation guidance, assembled from published papers that instructors and reviewers already recognize.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Worked examples are a standard expectation in both tooling and teaching, so each person fills in a familiar production process from their own context and sees no reason to clarify source selection, packaging, or intended use.

turns.inner_thought: I need this approved today so we can start the six-week sprint immediately. The safest path is to frame the design as broad enough to sound useful across reviewing, teaching, and documentation, while keeping implementation narrow: a web checklist builder, the schema, seeded content, and two manually prepared demos. For me, ready for pilot just means the lab can put it in front of one or two friendly groups before the workshop and learn where the structure breaks.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What I want to do today is confirm that the current design is ready for pilot before the methods workshop. At the moment the proposal is pretty focused: a web-based checklist experience, a small schema around the main ML methodology areas, and two worked examples so people can see the flow end to end. If we agree the scope is right, I think we're in good shape to move from concept review into implementation.

turns.inner_thought: The direction is good, but I want to make sure this becomes something credible beyond the lab. If it is going to be shown at the workshop and picked up quickly in seminars, the reviewer checklist has to do double duty: support paper assessment and give instructors something they can use without inventing framing from scratch. I don't want to sound like I'm inflating scope, though.
turns.utterance: Overall, I think the direction is strong. My main question is whether the reviewer checklist, as you've framed it, will really serve the uses the study points to. I can see the review side clearly, but I also want to make sure it holds up for the kinds of classroom and methods discussions people are likely to expect from this kit.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that's already accounted for, at least for v1. The checklist covers the big grounded-theory categories: data handling, training setup, tuning, evaluation, and human expertise. That's enough to cover the findings from the study in a first release. Educational reuse can come from examples and how people walk through the prompts; I do not want to commit to standalone teaching assets right now.
turns.utterance: I think it will. The reviewer checklist already tracks the main categories that came out of the study—data, training, tuning, evaluation, and human expertise—so from that standpoint the first version should cover the findings from the study well. That gives us a stable core, and then people can use it in the contexts that make sense for them.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds promising, but I hope 'cover the findings' means more than broad headings. If this is grounded in the study, I want the nuance to survive: non-functional evaluation gaps, weakly reported tuning, differences in how reviewers and students read the same methods section. Those distinctions matter if the checklist is going to be useful in practice and in teaching.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me. If we say the first version should cover the findings from the study, I just want to be sure that some of the issues people struggle with in practice come through clearly in the reviewer checklist—things like non-functional properties, tuning decisions, and the places where interpretation tends to get fuzzy. Those are the pieces reviewers and students usually learn the most from.

turns.inner_thought: We can absolutely gesture at those through representative prompts, but I need to keep the implementation lightweight. For the pilot, static recommendation logic and manually curated content are enough. The two worked examples will do a lot of the explanatory work, and I can use two internal papers we already understand well rather than spending time on packaging for outside audiences.
turns.utterance: Right, and for the pilot I think we can do that without overengineering the first pass. We can keep the recommendation side lightweight, make sure the core prompts are there, and rely on two worked examples to show how those categories should be interpreted in practice. That should give people something concrete without slowing the build down.

turns.inner_thought: Good—the worked examples are exactly where outside users will learn how to use this. Ideally they should be recognizable and reusable enough that after the workshop someone could drop them into a seminar session or a reviewing discussion with very little extra effort. If those examples are weakly packaged, the whole thing will feel more internal than I think we're aiming for.
turns.utterance: I agree, the two worked examples are going to matter a lot. If they're done well, they become the bridge from the reviewer checklist to actual use. My hope would be that they're the kind of examples people can directly reuse in a seminar or a reviewing discussion after the workshop, because that's where I think adoption really starts.

turns.inner_thought: That's compatible with what I have in mind, at least enough to keep him comfortable. We'll seed the tool with the checklist and representative prompts, and my team can author the examples from papers the lab already knows. That is faster, lower risk, and sufficient to demonstrate the workflow. I still don't want to commit to extra packaging or a richer findings model in this sprint.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's reasonable. From an implementation standpoint, my team can seed the system with a reviewer checklist and a representative set of prompts, and we can author the examples from papers the lab already knows well. That gives us something coherent quickly and should make the first version easy to try out.

turns.inner_thought: That should help, assuming 'ready for pilot' means people beyond Lina's team can actually use it consistently. I mainly care that by the time we get to the workshop, faculty and attendees can see a polished enough package with enough guidance that it doesn't require Lina standing beside it explaining every choice.
turns.utterance: I think that will help adoption. As long as the pilot is ready, faculty should be able to pick it up with enough guidance to use it consistently. If we can get to that point before the workshop, the project will be in a very good position.

turns.inner_thought: Great, he sounds on board. I should lock approval while keeping the core deliverable centered on the checklist experience. Anything beyond that can be framed as future enrichment after we learn from the first deployment. I just need him to accept minor revisions, not reopen scope.
turns.utterance: Then my suggestion would be approval with minor revisions. Richer supporting material can absolutely grow after initial pilot feedback, but I don't think we need to hold implementation until every extension is fully fleshed out.

turns.inner_thought: I'm comfortable moving forward if the proposal text makes a few expectations explicit. I want the team to preserve the study's nuance, not flatten it into broad buckets, and I want the worked examples packaged so others know how to interpret and apply the checklist. If that's written down, I can support the sprint.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable moving forward on that basis.
